html:
Swiss mercenaries were soldiers from the Swiss cantons hired out to foreign rulers, above all to the kings of France, from the late 1400s until the 1800s.

After the Burgundian Wars Swiss pikemen were thought the best infantry in Europe. The mountain cantons were poor, and selling soldiers brought money, pensions and trade privileges. Cantons signed contracts with France, Spain, the Dutch and the pope. Swiss often fought Swiss on opposite sides.

The trade drew criticism from reformers such as Zwingli. In 1792 hundreds of the Swiss Guards died defending the French king's palace in Paris. Recruiting for foreign armies was banned in 1859. One unit survives: the Pontifical Swiss Guard of the pope in Rome, founded in 1506.
sum: Swiss mercenaries were soldiers from the Swiss cantons hired out to foreign rulers, above all to the kings of France, from the late 1400s until the 1800s.
